title: Transformer-Based Preoperative Invasiveness Identification and Postoperative Recurrence Risk Stratification in Stage T1N0M0 Lung Adenocarcinoma: A Multi-Center Cohort Study.
abstract: Surgery is the primary curative treatment for early-stage lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), with accurate identification of tumor invasiveness critical for determining pulmonary resection extent. Due to significant variability in postoperative recurrence among early-stage LUAD patients with aggressive tumors, a more effective risk stratification system is urgently needed to improve prognosis. This study developed the T1LUT system, a transformer-based tool for T1N0M0 LUAD management, covering preoperative tumor invasiveness identification and postoperative recurrence risk stratification. Preoperatively, a 3D Vision Transformer (ViT) with extra learnable tokens analyzes CT images. It outperforms 3D ViT with only CLS tokens, 2D ViT, and 3D ResNet across three independent test centers (Center D: 0.896 vs. 0.892, 0.879, 0.836; Center E: 0.906 vs. 0.837, 0.837, 0.835; Center F: 0.884 vs. 0.884, 0.881, 0.861), achieving higher mean AUROC to accurately assess invasiveness and guide surgical resection extent. Postoperatively, the multimodal IAC-PR model integrates CT images, reports, pathological data, and clinical/demographic information. It stratifies invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC) patients into low-, medium-, or high-risk groups with an AUROC of 0.807 in testing-significantly better than single/partial-modal models. Validated via large-scale multicenter research, this system overcomes traditional assessment limitations, offering a robust tool for precise early LUAD treatment and improved prognosis.

title: Neuropathic Pain: From Mechanisms to Therapeutic Interventions.
abstract: Neuropathic pain is caused by injury or disease of the somatosensory system. It involves peripheral nerve injury, central sensitization, transmitter imbalance, glial activation, and large-scale network remodeling. Despite substantial advances in pain biology, clinical assessment continues to rely predominantly on patient-reported symptoms, sensory examination, and conventional neurophysiological testing, approaches that often fail to delineate the predominant biological mechanisms underlying pain in individual patients. Recent advances in sensory phenotyping and multimodal imaging have enabled in vivo characterization of abnormalities at the receptor, neuroinflammatory, and circuit levels, thereby providing a foundation for mechanism-based stratification and more individualized therapeutic decision-making. This review summarizes neuropathic pain from clinical stratification to mechanism-based imaging and therapeutic intervention. We describe key clinical dimensions, including sensory gain, sensory loss, peripheral and central pain generators, mixed nociceptive-neuropathic pain, central sensitization, and autonomic or small-fiber modifiers. These dimensions help explain why patients with the same diagnosis may show different symptoms and treatment responses. We also review major molecular mechanisms, including glutamatergic overactivity, GABAergic and glycinergic disinhibition, monoaminergic remodeling, and neuroimmune modulation. These changes reshape spinal, thalamocortical, limbic, salience, reward, cerebellar, and descending control circuits. Peripheral nerve ultrasound and MR neurography can help identify structural peripheral pain generators. PET, MRS, MRI, DTI, fMRI, EEG, and multimodal imaging can assess receptor availability, neurotransmitter balance, neuroinflammation, white matter integrity, and network connectivity. These imaging tools may link clinical phenotypes with biological mechanisms and help define mechanism-based subtypes. Imaging biomarkers may also support treatment selection, treatment monitoring, neuromodulation targeting, and translational trial design. This framework supports a shift from symptom-based assessment to mechanism-guided precision care for neuropathic pain.

title: Integrated Multi-Time-Point <sup>18</sup>F-FAPI PET/CT and Immune Histopathology for Predicting Pathological Complete Response in Microsatellite-Stable Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer Treated With Neoadjuvant Radiotherapy, Chemotherapy, and Immunotherapy.
abstract: Predicting pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy combined with immunotherapy and chemotherapy remains challenging in microsatellite-stable (MSS) locally advanced rectal cancer. In this prospective exploratory study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06608537), 49 patients received short-course radiotherapy followed by sintilimab plus CAPOX and subsequently underwent radical surgery. We investigated whether treatment response could be better characterized by integrating two complementary biological dimensions: baseline immune organization and treatment-related stromal remodeling captured by multi-time-point 1 8 F-FAPI PET/CT. The pCR rate was 49.0% (24/49), and serial 1 8 F-FAPI imaging revealed distinct stromal kinetic patterns between response groups. Integration of intratumoral tertiary lymphoid structure (iTLS) count, B-cell density, preoperative tumor-to-iliacus muscle ratio (TIMR) at 30 min, and the delayed TIMR retention index from 90 to 120 min (RI 34 ) yielded a four-variable model with a mean AUC of 0.874 in repeated nested cross-validation. Complementary preclinical experiments provided functional support for a CAF-TGFβ-B-cell/TLS axis linking stromal regulation, immune organization, and treatment resistance. These findings highlight the complementary value of spatial immune organization and dynamic FAPI-defined stromal kinetics and provide a biologically informed framework for post-neoadjuvant, preoperative response stratification, pending prospective multicenter validation.

title: Intratumoral and Peritumoral Functional Connectivity Reveals Network-Level Signatures of Glioma.
abstract: Gliomas are recognized as network-level diseases that remodel functional connectivity across the brain. Using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data from 306 patients with pathologically confirmed glioma at two hospitals, we delineated individualized intra- and peritumoral functional networks to quantify tumor-related alterations. Two novel indices-the ratio of intratumoral functional regions (RIFR) and ratio of peritumoral tumor-related regions (RPTR)-were proposed to describe network remodeling. Both indices were related to pathological, structural, functional, cognitive, language, and survival measures. Lower RIFR indicated diminished intratumoral connectivity and worse prognosis, while higher values reflected preserved network integration and longer survival. Models incorporating network features yielded areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.90 in training and 0.86-0.88 in external validation. Supporting analyses suggested that intratumoral functional regions are associated with distinct molecular and cellular characteristics. These findings suggest that intra- and peritumoral networks reflect biologically and functionally distinct tumor subregions and are associated with network-level alterations, brain function, and patient outcome. Interpretation is limited by the hemodynamic basis of rs-fMRI, incomplete data, and limited intraoperative validation. These findings identify individualized intra- and peritumoral connectivity measures as candidate markers of glioma-associated network remodeling and prognosis that require prospective, multimodal validation.

title: Accuracy of Machine Learning in Differential Diagnosis of Multiple System Atrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is frequently misdiagnosed as Parkinson's disease (PD) or progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), posing significant diagnostic challenges. Objective The aim of the study was to systematically evaluate the efficacy of machine learning (ML) in differentiating MSA from other neurodegenerative disorders. Methods We conducted a systematic search in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science (up to July 5, 2025), including ML-based MSA diagnostic studies. QUADAS-2 assessed bias risk, and a bivariate mixed-effects model synthesized diagnostic metrics. Results A total of 51 studies (comprising 3595 MSA patients and 18,189 total cases) were included in the systematic review. Of these, 38 studies contributed to the quantitative synthesis, whereas the remaining 13 studies were summarized qualitatively. In the primary analysis comparing MSA with PD, the pooled sensitivity was 0.86 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.81-0.90), specificity 0.87 (95% CI: 0.83-0.90), and the area under the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve (AUC) 0.93 (95% CI: 0.90-0.95). Overall, pooled sensitivity was 0.85 (95% CI: 0.82-0.88), specificity 0.92 (95% CI: 0.89-0.94), and AUC 0.94 (95% CI: 0.92-0.96). Positron emission tomography (PET)-based models achieved optimal performance (sensitivity: 0.90, specificity: 0.96, AUC: 0.97), whereas deep learning models outperformed others (sensitivity: 0.93, specificity: 0.98, AUC: 0.99). Conclusion ML models integrating PET/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy for MSA. Future work should prioritize prospective multicenter validation and standardized external testing to facilitate clinical implementation.

title: Preoperative Functional Imaging Predicts Deep Brain Stimulation Outcome in Craniocervical Dystonia.
abstract: Background Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established treatment for craniocervical dystonia (CCD), yet postoperative benefit varies widely and cannot be estimated before surgery. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has shown prognostic value across DBS indications. The objective of this study was to develop and externally validate preoperative rs-fMRI models estimating DBS response in CCD. Methods Forty-two patients from two independent centers underwent preoperative 3 T rs-fMRI (discovery, n = 26; validation, n = 16). Using 12 literature-informed, symptom-relevant regions of interest, we quantified the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation as a measure of intrinsic regional neural activity. We applied regularized modeling to classify super-responders, distinguish responders from non-responders, and estimate improvement in Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale motor subscore. Results When applied to the validation cohort, the imaging models achieved a three-category classification accuracy of 75.0% (50.5%-89.8%) using a sequential two-step procedure (P perm = 0.002). Predicted continuous improvement was also correlated with empirical improvement (R ext = 0.65, Q 2 = 0.34, P perm = 0.004). Within the discovery cohort, nested leave-one-out-cross-validation, in which feature selection and decision-threshold derivation were repeated independently within each training fold, yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.73 (0.50-0.96) and 0.77 (0.51-1.00). Across models, baseline primary motor cortex activity was consistently associated with diminished postoperative benefit. Conclusions Preoperative rs-fMRI captures clinically relevant variation in baseline brain state in CCD, with predictive performance supported in an external validation. These findings provide preliminary support for rs-fMRI as a potential source of information to aid patient counseling and clinical decision-making, pending prospective validation. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Automated Magnetic Resonance Volumetry to Measure Multiple System Atrophy Disease Progression in Clinical Trials.
abstract: Background Recent studies have reported longitudinal brain atrophy in multiple system atrophy (MSA) in relatively small patient cohorts. Objective To compare longitudinal regional brain volume and clinical changes as endpoint measures for MSA clinical trials. Methods MSA patients with 1-year longitudinal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were selected from the placebo arm of the M-STAR Study (NCT03952806) and stratified into MSA-cerebellar (MSA-C) and MSA-parkinsonism (MSA-P) subtypes. A multisite healthy control (HC) cohort from international datasets was included for comparison. Baseline and longitudinal atrophy were assessed through automated MRI volumetry. Standardized longitudinal effect size values with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and sample sizes required to detect treatment effect were estimated for 42 individual regional brain volumes, four combined volumetric indexes, nine clinical scales, and serum neurofilament light chain. Results The final study cohort included 129 MSA patients (76 MSA-C, 53 MSA-P) and 184 HC. The most atrophic structures at baseline were infratentorial regions in MSA-C and putamen in MSA-P. In both subtypes, infratentorial structures showed the largest longitudinal volume loss compared with HC. The annualized change of a cerebellum-pons-putamen volumetric index was the most powerful progression biomarker in MSA patients (effect size: -1.81 [95% CI: -2.14, -1.55]) and in both subtypes (MSA-C: -2.04 [95% CI: -2.58, -1.68], MSA-P: -1.55 [95% CI: -2.08, -1.22]), requiring the lowest sample size per arm (MSA, N = 55 to detect 30% treatment effect), and outperforming clinical measures (-59.6% patients required per arm). Conclusion These findings support longitudinal MRI-derived regional atrophy rates as sensitive imaging endpoints to assess treatment efficacy in MSA clinical trials. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Identification of Variants in Two Families With Congenital Cataract by Whole Exome Sequencing.
abstract: Background Congenital cataract (CC) is an ophthalmic disorder diagnosed at birth or during early infancy, characterized by severe visual impairment and potential blindness. This study aimed to evaluate the pathogenicity of two variants: GJA8 c.201C>G (p.Asp67Glu) and CRYBB2 c.325A>T (p.Ile109Phe). Methods The patient's lenses were examined using slit-lamp photography and B-ultrasound. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) and sanger sequencing were performed to identify the variants. Multiple sequence alignment was conducted using CLUSTALW to assess the evolutionary conservation of the affected residues. Structural modeling and conformational analyzes of wild-type (WT) and mutant-type (MT) proteins were conducted using AlphaFold2, PyMOL, and computational structural dynamics approaches, including root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) and normal mode analysis (NMA). Results Two likely pathogenic missense variants were identified in two unrelated families: c.201C>G (p.Asp67Glu) in exon 2 of GJA8, which encodes Connexin 50 (Cx50) protein, was paternally inherited in family 1, whereas c.325A>T (p.Ile109Phe) in exon 4 of CRYBB2 occurred de novo in family 2. The c.201C>G (p.Asp67Glu) variant mapped to the first extracellular loop (EL1) of Cx50. Structural modeling revealed disruption of the Asp67-Arg185 ionic interaction (Cα-OD distance: 3.4 → 4.9 Å) alongside a novel hydrogen bond with Asn63. Reduced RMSF in the mutant indicated localized rigidification of EL1, potentially impairing channel gating and correlating with severe cataract in affected family members. The co-segregation of the variant with the affected phenotype within the family 1 was confirmed by sanger sequencing combined with phenotypic analysis. The c.325A>T variant (p.Ile109Phe) in CRYBB2 increased protein flexibility, and the bulky aromatic phenylalanine side chain perturbed the hydrophobic core of Greek key motif III, causing global dynamic instability. The CRYBB2 c.325A>T variant was further confirmed to be de novo by sanger sequencing in conjunction with phenotypic analysis in family 2. Furthermore, multiple sequence alignment demonstrated that both residues are highly evolutionarily conserved. Conclusions This study expands the pathogenic spectrum of congenital cataract. Our findings provide novel insights into the molecular diagnosis of CC and have important implications for genetic counseling.

title: Free Innervated Gracilis Muscular Flap for Functional Abdominal Wall Reconstruction Following Desmoid Tumor Resection: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Desmoid tumors (DTs) are rare, benign, locally aggressive myofibroblastic neoplasms. Complete resection with negative margins remains the standard treatment despite their lack of metastatic potential. As DT commonly involve the anterior abdominal wall, their excision may result in complex defects requiring advanced reconstruction. We herein present the first functional single-stage reconstruction of an abdominal wall defect with the use of a free innervated gracilis muscle flap transfer. A 29-year-old woman, presented with a palpable tumor on the left-side of her abdominal wall. She underwent surgery and on biopsy, the tumor was diagnosed as a DT. title: Simultaneous T1, T2, R2*, PDFF, and triglyceride quantification in the head and neck using magnetic resonance fingerprinting on a 1.5T MR-Linac.
abstract: Background The extraction of quantitative biomarkers on the MR-Linac, which have been shown to be promising in the head and neck, remains a significant challenge due to the strict time constraints. Purpose The purpose of this study was to assess the technical feasibility of magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF) to simultaneously extract quantitative T1, T2, R2*, PDFF, and triglyceride composition in the head and neck on the MR-Linac. Methods Inversion-prepared, multi-echo, golden angle radial, variable flip angle, MRF data were acquired on a 1.5T MR-Linac. The data were corrected for phase errors in the bipolar multi-echo acquisition followed by low rank reconstruction with total variation regularization. A dictionary of signals parameterized by T1/T2 was calculated with an extended phase graph algorithm. The singular images were constructed using a signal subspace from the dictionary and the first singular images were then jointly fit for R2* and PDFF using the off-resonance information from an independent B0 map. The complete set of B0/T2*-corrected fat-water separated water singular images were fitted for T1/T2. Triglyceride composition was computed using the multi-echo complex readout. Three phantoms and three healthy volunteers were assessed for accuracy, repeatability, and reproducibility against validated reference sequences across five days using a test-retest setup. Results All coefficients of determination were at least 0.9 against reference sequences in standard phantoms across all quantitative parameters. The repeatability and reproducibility averaged under 5% in phantoms and under 10% in healthy volunteers. Conclusion The proposed MRF acquisition demonstrated the potential to replace the current time-intensive sequences on the 1.5T MR-Linac, thus increasing the adoption of specialized quantitative imaging biomarker approaches at high temporal density in the head and neck.

title: Combined PET imaging of tumor hypoxia and proliferation in Glioblastoma using a single injection of 18F-FMISO and 18F-FLT: Association with sites of subsequent recurrence.
abstract: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intra-tumoral heterogeneity, rapid proliferation, hypoxia-driven radio-resistance, and early recurrence. Gadolinium-Enhanced MRI, the standard of care imaging modality for surgical and radiotherapy planning, lacks specificity for viable tumor burden, particularly in non-enhancing regions. Purpose This pilot study aimed to evaluate whether preoperative dual-tracer PET using a combined dose of 18 FMISO (hypoxia) and 18 FLT (proliferation) improves tumor delineation and predicts subsequent local recurrence compared with MRI. Methods Seven patients with WHO grade 4 gliomas (5 GBM, 2 IDH-mutant astrocytomas) underwent preoperative dual-[FMISO+FLT] static PET at 180 min post-injection, and MRI. 6/7 patients underwent resection. Tumor volumes were segmented from PET, contrast-enhanced T1 (T1-Gd), and T2-FLAIR. Postoperative resection cavities were delineated, and follow-up MRI every 3 months was used to identify recurrence. PET-defined tumor volumes extending beyond resection were correlated with subsequent recurrence sites. Results Thirteen lesions were analyzed; all showed [FMISO+FLT] uptake (mean activity concentration ratio 1.6 with the cerebellar cortex used as reference region). PET-defined tumor volumes (9.2 cc) were slightly larger than T1-Gd (7.9 cc) but smaller than T2-FLAIR (28.8 cc). PET-defined volumes frequently extended beyond MRI-defined contours (mean non-overlap 6.4 cc vs T1-Gd; 1.5 cc vs. T2-FLAIR). Of six patients undergoing resection, four developed local recurrence within 3.3 months. In all cases, recurrence arose within PET-avid regions outside the resection cavity. The other two patients with complete resection of PET-defined volumes showed a relatively prolonged progression-free-survival (PFS) and including one patient with overall survival exceeding 36 months. Conclusions Dual-[FMISO+FLT] PET is feasible, safe, and can allow delineation of biologically viable tumor subregions, in particular within the MRI T2-FLAIR volume. This approach prospectively identified sites of subsequent local recurrence and may improve surgical planning and radiotherapy dose escalation. Larger validation studies are warranted to establish dual-tracer PET as a precision imaging paradigm in GBM.

title: Multimodal PET/MRI radiomics model for the classification of Alzheimer's disease and other dementia subtypes: A multicenter study.
abstract: Background Accurate and early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains a major clinical challenge. This study aims to explore the value of multimodal positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics to improve diagnostic accuracy. Purpose To develop and evaluate hippocampus-based multimodal PET/MRI radiomics models for AD classification and exploratory five-class classification, and to compare early fusion (EF) with multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM)-based decision-level fusion. Method A total of 758 patients who underwent both PET ([18F]FDG and Amyloid-β) and MRI (3DT1, T1WI, T2WI, T2-FLAIR) were retrospectively included as the primary dataset in this study. 945 radiomic features (RFs) per sequence were extracted from the bilateral hippocampus. Models were evaluated on the primary cohort using a five-fold stratified cross-validation at the subject level (80% training and 20% testing in each fold). Feature selection was performed independently for each sequence using the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO). For multimodal PET/MR models, features from all six sequences were concatenated, and feature selection was applied (EF). Six classifiers were used to construct classification models for two tasks, including (1) AD/non-AD classification, and (2) exploratory five-class classification among AD, FTD, VaD, MCI, and other dementia. In addition, an MCDM-based strategy was implemented to fuse multimodal RFs and multi-classifiers. Modality-matched external validation was performed in an independent cohort of 45 patients with 3DT1 and Aβ PET available. Decision curve analysis (DCA) was employed to assess the clinical usefulness of the models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied to explore the interpretability of the EF-based model. Results Among the 758 patients in the primary dataset, AD, FTD, VaD, and MCI were present in 481 (63.5%), 34 (4.5%), 15 (2.0%), 136 (17.9%) cases, with 92 (12.1%) classified as the other dementia subtypes. The MCDM-based models achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) for both tasks on the primary dataset (Task 1: AUC = 0.848; Task 2: AUC = 0.797), significantly higher than EF-based models in Task 2 (AUC = 0.782, p < 0.001) and showing comparable performance in Task 1 (AUC = 0.839, p = 0.629). On the external dataset, EF and MCDM models achieved AUCs of 0.741 and 0.761, respectively, for Task 1. The MCDM model showed a higher AUC than EF. DCA suggested potential net-benefit advantages for the multimodal models across selected threshold ranges. SHAP analysis identified wavelet-transformed texture features as the key predictors. Conclusion Hippocampus-based PET/MRI radiomics models showed promising performance for binary AD classification, with further improvement achieved by the MCDM strategy. The five-class findings should be regarded as exploratory. External validation provides preliminary support for the reduced 3DT1-Aβ PET model and does not establish the generalizability of the complete six-modality framework.

title: Deep learning-based CNN method for fiducial marker detection in kilovoltage X-ray images for liver tumor motion monitoring.
abstract: During radiation therapy, liver tumor motion can reduce dose delivery accuracy and increase irradiation of adjacent healthy tissues. Because liver tumors are difficult to visualize directly on kilovoltage (kV) X-ray images, fiducial markers are commonly implanted as surrogates for tumor position during treatment. Conventional marker-segmentation approaches such as template matching can lose accuracy when markers are obscured by bone, surgical clips, or stents. Although Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based approaches have shown strong performance for image analysis, their application has been constrained to more static organs such as the prostate or has used single-center and vendor-specific datasets, limiting assessment of model transportability across different institutions and anatomic sites. The aim of this study was to develop, integrate, and evaluate a CNN-based method for fiducial marker detection in kV X-ray images to support real-time image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT) during liver radiotherapy using a multi-institutional, multi-platform dataset spanning both large and fast free-breathing motion and slow and small breath-hold motion. A compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was trained on 314,625 kilovoltage (kV) X-ray images encompassing 28 patients from the multi-institutional TROG 17.03 LARK clinical trial (NCT02984566). The model was validated using a hold-out set of 31,463 images (10%) from the same cohort of 12 patients and 55 treatment fractions, spanning three centers and three respiratory motion-management techniques. The CNN was tested on 4184 images from 16 patients and 55 fractions across three centers and three motion-management techniques. The ground truth for testing was manually segmented marker positions from every 10 degrees of gantry rotation for each fraction of each test patient. Based on AAPM guidelines (TG147 and TGB135.B), feasibility for clinical implementation was predefined as > 95% of marker positions being within 2 mm of the ground truth position in each dimension, and processing time less than 150 ms per image using a simulated real-time Kilovoltage Intrafraction Monitoring (KIM) framework. Additional evaluation metrics included sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUC). For the unseen test patient data, the marker position was segmented by the CNN within 2 mm in 95.4% of frames on the X axis and 97.6% of frames on the Y axis, meeting AAPM criteria. Sensitivity reached 97.76%, specificity was 99.94%, and the AUC was 0.9964. No statistically significant difference in localization error was observed between breath-hold and free-breathing treatments, although this comparison was limited by the small number of free-breathing patients. Localization error differed significantly between Varian and Elekta linacs due to imbalance within the dataset. The processing time for each image was 50-60 ms using a NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 GPU. A CNN-based method for fiducial marker detection in the liver was developed and evaluated on multi-institutional kV X-ray images spanning free-breathing and breath-hold motion, as well as Varian and Elekta linac platforms. The method satisfied the predefined feasibility criteria for positional accuracy and computation time, supporting future translation toward clinical implementation.

title: Quantitative and qualitative magnetic resonance imaging-based analysis to predict postoperative disease progression in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Background Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most common abdominal malignancies and the third leading cause of cancer-related death globally. Predicting the postoperative prognosis of HCC remains an important area of clinical research. Many qualitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicators have been used for noninvasive and global assessment of HCC for diagnostic and prognostic purposes. However, the prognostic value of quantitative MRI parameters has not been extensively validated in multicenter cohorts. Objective This study aimed to verify whether MRI-based imaging features could improve prognostic prediction in patients with HCC. We developed prognostic models to predict the progression-free survival (PFS) of patients with HCC. Methods In this multicenter cohort study, 203 patients diagnosed with early- to intermediate-stage HCC were divided into a training dataset and an external validation dataset. In addition to clinical indicators, the candidates included qualitative and quantitative MRI data. Three noninvasive models were developed: the Clinical Model, the Radiological Model, and the Combined Model. The patients were stratified according to the risk of disease progression. Model performance was assessed through discrimination and calibration analyses, decision curve analysis was performed, and a clinical application was designed. In addition, the subgroups at different stages of the disease were analyzed, and PFS was compared between the high- and low-risk groups. Results Prognostic nutritional index, tumor-feeding vessels, mosaic architecture and the signal enhancement ratio (SER) parameter were identified as independent predictors of disease progression in patients with HCC. The Combined Model demonstrated superior performance compared with the Clinical and Radiological Models. The areas under the curve (AUCs) in the training dataset were 0.822, 0.748, and 0.795, whereas those in the validation dataset were 0.819, 0.758, and 0.677, respectively. The Combined Model also demonstrated favorable calibration and greater net clinical benefit on decision curve analysis. Its predictive ability remained consistent regardless of the Child-Pugh classification or Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer stage. Conclusion This study highlights the important role of quantitative and qualitative MRI assessments in evaluating the prognosis of patients with HCC and emphasizes the predictive value of SER parameter. However, these findings should nevertheless be interpreted with caution given the relatively limited sample size, despite the use of bootstrap internal validation and external validation.

title: A two-stage framework for fast proton spot map generation in pencil beam scanning prostate SBRT planning.
abstract: Background In pencil beam scanning (PBS) proton therapy, treatment plans are encoded as proton spot maps (PSMs). Although deep-learning methods can rapidly predict three-dimensional (3D) dose distributions from patient anatomy and planning intent, there is still no widely adopted direct, non-iterative approach to convert doses into physically deliverable spot patterns. This limits end-to-end automation in treatment planning and adaptive replanning for PBS. Purpose We developed and retrospectively evaluated GenSpot, a two-stage framework that reconstructs a PBS PSM from CT and dose. This study focused on the dose-to-spots reconstruction step under controlled, achievable-dose conditions, using clinical Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions as input in a single-institution prostate stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) cohort. Methods GenSpot uses a physics-informed projected proton spot map (PrPSM) representation that projects individual proton spots through the CT using water-equivalent thickness and percentage depth dose (PDD) information, aligning the spots with the CT and dose voxel grid while preserving a linear relationship with spot weights. Our dataset comprised 1036 fields from 259 prostate SBRT plans, split into training, validation, and test sets in an 80%/10%/10% ratio. A 3D SwinUNETR model was trained to predict PrPSMs from CT and dose inputs. Field-specific PSMs were then reconstructed from the predicted PrPSMs using column-wise nonnegative Lasso regression with precomputed PDD curves. MC dose distributions from GenSpot and clinical PSMs were compared using voxel-wise mean absolute error (MAE), 3D gamma analysis (3%/3 mm, 10% low-dose threshold), and dose-volume histogram (DVH) metrics at the composite-plan level. Results Within the held-out test dataset, the selected SwinUNETR model achieved a mean PrPSM MAE of 0.06 ± 0.02 (normalized units) with high structural similarity to projected clinical PrPSMs. At the dose level, MC doses from GenSpot PSMs showed low MAE (0.07 ± 0.03 Gy in the nonzero-dose region) and high mean gamma passing rates (0.92 ± 0.05 at the field level and 0.99 ± 0.02 at the plan level). Composite-plan DVH metrics differences were generally within 1 Gy for targets and organs at risk, although the high-dose tail of the clinical target volume showed a modest systematic increase. Spot map complexity, measured by the number of energy layers and spot counts, was similar to that of clinical plans, with 20% more spots for GenSpot PSMs. For a four-field case, GenSpot PSM generation required approximately 2.9 ± 0.2 min excluding final MC recalculation. Conclusions GenSpot reconstructed machine-compatible PSMs from CT and clinical MC dose with close composite-plan dose agreement in a single-institution prostate SBRT cohort. These results support GenSpot as a rapid, physics-informed dose-to-spots reconstruction component under achievable-dose conditions. The present study does not establish performance for arbitrary predicted or adapted dose inputs, and final MC recalculation and standard QA remain required before clinical use. Further validation with non-idealized dose inputs, multi-institution data, higher-resolution dose representations, and dedicated optimization-based baselines is needed before broader clinical implementation.

title: Radiogenomic inference of transcription factor regulatory architecture associated with a high-risk CT phenotype in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To determine whether a CT radiomics-defined poor-prognosis phenotype in NSCLC is associated with reproducible transcriptomic programs and distinct transcription factor (TF) activity patterns. Methods This retrospective radiogenomic study used public datasets from The Cancer Imaging Archive. A prognostic radiomics model was developed from pretreatment CT in 402 patients from the NSCLC-Radiomics collection and evaluated in an independent cohort of 110 patients from the NSCLC Radiogenomics collection. Seven tumor-centered intra- and peritumoral regions were analyzed. Features were extracted from original, wavelet-, and Laplacian-of-Gaussian-filtered CT images. After preprocessing and training-cohort standardization, a LASSO-penalized Cox model was developed. The locked model retained eight features, all from the GTV+10-mm region, and was applied to the internal and external validation cohorts without refitting. The training-cohort median RadScore was used unchanged for Kaplan-Meier visualization. Matched transcriptomic data were analyzed using preranked gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), gene set variation analysis (GSVA), target-gene-based TF activity inference, TF co-activity networks, exploratory regulator prioritization, unsupervised TF-state clustering, and LINCS-based perturbational analysis. Results The radiomics model achieved Harrell concordance indices of 0.785 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.767-0.793), 0.819 (95% CI, 0.788-0.833), and 0.785 (95% CI, 0.752-0.802) in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. The high-risk phenotype showed exploratory enrichment of proliferative and stress-adaptive programs, led by HALLMARK_E2F_TARGETS (normalized enrichment score [NES] = 1.696, false discovery rate [FDR] = 0.045), with additional enrichment of MYC targets and inflammatory response. HALLMARK_HYPOXIA showed a positive directional trend but did not meet the prespecified exploratory threshold. GSVA provided complementary sample-level evidence for MYC targets, hypoxia, E2F targets, DNA repair, and cell-cycle activity. Eleven of 13 evaluated TFs met the prespecified FDR threshold, including YAP1, MYC, HIF1A, E2F3, STAT3, KLF4, E2F1, and TP53. Integrated analysis prioritized HIF1A, STAT3, TP53, YAP1, and E2F1/E2F3 as candidate regulatory nodes. Unsupervised clustering of all 110 radiogenomic patients, performed independently of radiomics risk labels, identified three exploratory TF-defined states: Hypoxia_Metabolic (n = 69), Cell_Cycle_E2F (n = 31), and Hippo_Mechanosensing (n = 10). LINCS-based analysis generated regulatory-state-associated compound hypotheses. Conclusions A CT radiomics-defined poor-prognosis phenotype in NSCLC is associated with coherent transcriptomic programs and an interpretable TF regulatory architecture. This framework links routine imaging phenotypes to latent tumor-control programs and supports regulatory-state-informed therapeutic hypothesis generation.

title: Artificial intelligence apps for medical image analysis using pyCERR and cancer genomics cloud.
abstract: Purpose To provide a software resource that enables medical researchers and practitioners to develop and apply reproducible, out-of-the-box, AI-based analysis workflows for radiological and radiotherapy data. Development and validation methods The framework comprises two main components: the Python-native computational environment for radiological research (pyCERR) for radiological image processing, and the cancer genomics cloud (CGC), a National Cancer Institute-funded resource that supports cloud-hosted collaborative projects, with tools for managing collaborators and compute-hardware from providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. pyCERR is open-source (GNU GPL) and distributed at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr; it provides user-friendly data structures, simplified access to metadata across radiological imaging modalities, and tools for data transformation, AI-based image segmentation, radiomics, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI analysis, radiotherapy dose-volume histogram (DVH) feature extraction, and normal-tissue complication and tumor-control models. Radiomics features comply with the Image biomarker standardization initiative (IBSI) standards and are validated against published reference values. Unit tests covering data input/output, radiomics, DVH features, and visualization run on every code update. Workflows are containerized for reproducible, identical execution on the CGC and on local hardware. The CGC enables AI inference from radiological images to be combined with other data types such as genomics and proteomics. Our public CGC project (https://cgc.sbgenomics.com/u/sevenbridges/pycerr-radiological-radiotherapy-imageanalysis), accessible with free registration, currently includes apps for organ-at-risk (OAR) and lung-nodule segmentation based on published models trained in-house and clinically validated. These apps can be run interactively from a web browser or programmatically via a REST API with client support for multiple programming languages. Notebooks demonstrating the CGC API and pyCERR capabilities are provided at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr-notebooks. Potential applications The framework facilitates end-to-end radiological image analysis and reproducible research, including data access from public and private repositories, training and inference with AI models, and utilities for data management, visualization, and simplified access to image metadata.

title: Self-supervised multi-contrast MRI reconstruction via mask-guided frequency-domain fusion.
abstract: Background Multi-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MC-MRI) enables detailed tissue characterization by acquiring multiple contrast-weighted images from the same anatomical region. Redundancy across contrasts can improve reconstruction from under-sampled data. However, conventional deep learning approaches rely on fully-sampled, contrast-aligned datasets, which require long acquisition times. Extended scanning durations not only increase patient burden but may also introduce physiological risks, limiting the practical adoption of accelerated MC-MRI in clinical settings. Purpose This study introduces Self-MF, a self-supervised MC-MRI reconstruction framework that leverages contrast redundancy without requiring fully sampled target-contrast labels. The framework aims to provide a high-fidelity, scalable solution for reconstructing under-sampled multi-contrast images while preserving anatomical details and contrast fidelity. Methods Self-MF implements a contrast-aware self-supervised learning strategy that randomly partitions the acquired target k-space into input and held-out subsets, allowing the model to learn joint anatomical priors from under-sampled data without fully sampled target-contrast labels. A mask-guided frequency-domain conditioning module constructs reference-conditioned auxiliary frequency channels from auxiliary contrasts and acquired target measurements, enhancing the recovery of fine structural features during score-based reconstruction. Experiments were conducted on public datasets (IXI, fastMRI) and a clinical multi-coil dataset (SIAT), spanning multiple acceleration factors and undersampling patterns to assess robustness and generalizability. Results Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that Self-MF outperforms existing representative reconstruction methods across different contrasts, datasets, and acceleration factors. On the SIAT multi-contrast dataset, Self-MF achieved PSNR/SSIM values of 35.16/0.8870, 33.46/0.9054, and 35.31/0.9187 for T1WI, T2WI, and PDWI reconstruction under 2D random undersampling at R = 4, respectively. On the fastMRI brain dataset, Self-MF achieved 41.15 dB/0.9637 and 35.02 dB/0.8814 for T2WI reconstruction under R = 4 and R = 8, respectively, consistently outperforming the compared classical, learning-based, and diffusion-based baselines. Conclusions Self-MF provides an effective, self-supervised solution for high-fidelity MC-MRI reconstruction without fully sampled target-contrast labels. By combining contrast-aware self-supervision, frequency-domain conditioning, and diffusion-based reconstruction, the framework achieves superior image quality and robust anatomical preservation, representing a significant advancement for multi-contrast MRI in both research and clinical practice.

A mask-guided frequency-domain conditioning module constructs reference-conditioned auxiliary frequency channels from auxiliary contrasts and acquired target measurements, enhancing the recovery of fine structural features during score-based reconstruction. Experiments were conducted on public datasets (IXI, fastMRI) and a clinical multi-coil dataset (SIAT), spanning multiple acceleration factors and undersampling patterns to assess robustness and generalizability.

Results

Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that Self-MF outperforms existing representative reconstruction methods across different contrasts, datasets, and acceleration factors. On the SIAT multi-contrast dataset, Self-MF achieved PSNR/SSIM values of 35.16/0.8870, 33.46/0.9054, and 35.31/0.9187 for T1WI, T2WI, and PDWI reconstruction under 2D random undersampling at R = 4, respectively. On the fastMRI brain dataset, Self-MF achieved 41.15 dB/0.9637 and 35.02 dB/0.8814 for T2WI reconstruction under R = 4 and R = 8, respectively, consistently outperforming the compared classical, learning-based, and diffusion-based baselines.

Conclusions

Self-MF provides an effective, self-supervised solution for high-fidelity MC-MRI reconstruction without fully sampled target-contrast labels. title: Convolutional neural network metal artifact reduction in ultra-high resolution photon counting detector CT of middle- and inner-ear implants.
abstract: Background Metallic inner- and middle-ear implants with submillimeter structures requiring ultra-high resolution (UHR) imaging invariably result in metal artifacts at CT, which can obscure adjacent microstructures and subtle pathologic findings. Current metal artifact reduction techniques can be less effective for small metal objects or metal in heterogeneous background anatomy, and can sometimes introduce new artifacts or noise. Purpose To develop and evaluate an image-domain convolutional neural network to reduce metal artifacts near inner- and middle-ear implants in UHR photon-counting-detector (PCD)-CT. Methods For network training, three stapes prosthesis models containing titanium and platinum were randomly oriented within a head-sized phantom and imaged on a PCD-CT with a UHR protocol. Metal and metal+artifact images were isolated by subtraction of the phantom background followed by CT number thresholding. Isolated artifact signal was enhanced via multiplication with a randomized factor ranging from one to a pre-determined artifact amplification scalar hyperparameter. Paired training inputs (with artifacts) and labels (without artifacts) were created by adding metal-free patient temporal bone images with metal+artifact and metal images, respectively. Combinations of 9 patient CT volumes and 24 metal CT volumes were used to create 216 CT volumes for training and validation with an 80%/20% training/validation split. The network was retrained with different amplification scalars (5, 10, 20, 30, 40) and with either mean-squared-error or mean-absolute-error loss functions to determine the optimal combination of these hyperparameters. The network was tested on 7 CT volumes from patients with three different implant types: stapes prostheses, cochlear implants, and a transverse sinus stent. Network performance was quantified through the artifact index, noise magnitude, CT number preservation of metal and bone, and dimensions of metal measured as the full-width at half-maximum of CT number line profiles. Results Networks trained with mean-squared-error demonstrated a trade-off between metal artifact reduction and preservation of bone CT number as the artifact amplification scalar changed. The trade-off was not observed when mean-absolute error was used. Using the network with hyperparameters that best preserved bone and reduced artifacts simultaneously (mean-absolute-error, amplification scalar 20), the artifact index was improved by 83.2% (p < 0.001) across all implant types, and image noise was reduced by 46.8% (p < 0.001). Artifact reduction was significantly better for cases with stapes prostheses than the other implant types (p < 0.004), although artifact index was still greatly improved for all implant types (91.1% for the stapes prostheses, 81.3% for the CI, and 72.9% for the transverse sinus stent). Metal implant dimensions were not significantly different between the network input and output images (p = 0.67). Conclusion An image-domain convolutional neural network with task-specific hyperparameters reduced artifact severity and image noise in UHR PCD-CT of different inner- and middle-ear implants without loss of fine image detail.

title: Evaluation of quantitative accuracy in 4D DCE-bCT: Insights from a perfusion phantom study.
abstract: Background Four-dimensional dynamic contrast-enhanced breast CT (4D DCE-bCT) provides submillimeter spatial resolution and temporal sampling within seconds, offering potential for improved perfusion assessment in breast cancer. Its quantitative accuracy, however, must be validated. Purpose To evaluate the accuracy of dynamic iodine concentration quantification in 4D DCE-bCT using a perfusion phantom with in-line optical spectroscopy and ultraviolet-visible (UV/VIS) spectrophotometry as reference standards. Methods A dynamic flow phantom with a 3 mm internal diameter was used to approximate tumor-feeding vessels. Potassium iodide (KI) contrast was introduced using block-pulse injections at 1, 3, and 5 mg I/mL and a gradual inflow-outflow protocol to reproduce bolus passage. In-line optical spectroscopy and UV/VIS spectrophotometry provided reference measurements. Dynamic bCT acquisitions were performed using a previously developed sparse-view protocol. A static pre-contrast scan was reconstructed with the iterative maximum-likelihood polychromatic algorithm for CT (IMPACT), and post-contrast dynamic scans were reconstructed using the prior image constrained compressed sensing (PICCS) algorithm. Acquisitions were performed at 65 kV with 0.25 mm Cu filtration, 80 mA for the pre-contrast scan (300 projections over 10 s) and 32 mA for the post-contrast scans (444 projections per 100 s), using a 5 ms pulse width. Projection data were corrected for scatter and motion before reconstruction, and the static prior was then subtracted from post-contrast volumes. Object-size effects were evaluated using the 3 mm tube and 5, 10, 15, and 20 mm hollow spheres filled with non-flowing iodine at 1, 3, and 5 mg I/mL. The tube interior was segmented using thresholding and morphological cleanup, while spherical phantoms were segmented by identifying the sphere center and extracting all enclosed voxels. Voxel values were converted to iodine concentration using a pre-determined calibration curve, and agreement with reference standards was evaluated using peak concentrations and time-concentration profiles, with errors reported as absolute and relative differences. Results In dynamic block-pulse experiments, peak iodine concentrations measured by 4D DCE-bCT were systematically underestimated relative to ground truth, with relative errors of approximately 12% to 39%. In gradual inflow-outflow experiments, the peak iodine concentration derived from 4D DCE-bCT was 5.24 ± 0.61 mg I/mL, whereas optical ground truth measured 5.17 mg I/mL. Static experiments demonstrated an average underestimation of 0.23 ± 0.14 mg I/mL across target sizes and concentrations and no relationship between iodine estimation and target size. Conclusion 4D DCE-bCT enabled acquisition of time-varying iodine concentration profiles in a 3 mm tube phantom. Gradual changes were captured more accurately compared to rapid changes, consistent with temporal averaging. These results demonstrate the feasibility of dynamic iodine imaging with 4D DCE-bCT while highlighting current limitations and motivating further evaluation in anatomically realistic phantoms and pilot clinical studies.

title: A dual-prompt framework combining spatial-mask priors and clinical-text conditioning for CT-only GTV delineation in esophageal cancer: A multicenter study.
abstract: Background Accurate gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation is essential for esophageal cancer radiotherapy, but CT-only automatic delineation remains difficult because of indistinct tumor boundaries. Purpose This study aimed to develop and validate a two-stage dual-prompt framework combining a spatial-mask prior with LLaMA3-encoded clinical-text conditioning for primary esophageal GTV delineation. Methods This multicenter study included 857 patients: 500 for development, 125 for internal validation, 50 for ablation analysis, and 182 for external validation. The proposed framework consists of two stages: (1) a CT-based automatic segmentation network generating an initial GTV as a spatial mask prompt, and (2) a refinement network that jointly incorporates spatial mask prompt and LLaMA3-encoded clinical text prompt derived from structured clinical information. Performance was evaluated using overlap, surface distance, and volumetric metrics, and compared with multiple state-of-the-art deep learning models. Ablation and radiomics analyses assessed component contributions and downstream consistency. Results In internal validation, the framework achieved a DSC of 80.32 ± 6.65%, an HD95 of 11.42 ± 8.90 mm, and an absolute volume difference of 9.99 ± 10.49 mL; all Holm-adjusted p values were <0.001 versus the comparison models. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the external cohorts. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the two external cohorts, respectively. In external cohort A, ContextUNETR showed a lower mean HD95 than the proposed model (10.93 ± 8.03 vs. 13.44 ± 18.90 mm), although the paired difference was not statistically significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.906). Compared with the direct Stage-1 output, the complete framework consistently improved overlap, boundary-distance, and volumetric-agreement metrics across the internal and both external validation cohorts (all adjusted p < 0.001). LLaMA3 encoding improved DSC versus an MLP using the same variables (adjusted p = 0.009), whereas ASSD did not differ significantly. Automatic and manual GTVs showed high radiomic concordance and comparable prognostic performance. Conclusion The framework improved overlap and volumetric agreement for CT-only primary esophageal GTV delineation across multicenter validation cohorts, although boundary-distance performance varied across external cohorts.

title: Joint segmentation and landmark detection for cardiac MRI with multi-scale inter-task feature fusion and gradient-bridged anatomical constraints.
abstract: Segmentation and landmark detection are essential yet complex tasks in Cardiac MRI (CMR) for quantitative assessment of the heart. Existing automatic CMR analysis methods typically handle the two tasks independently, overlooking their synergies that could improve the performance of both tasks. To develop an accurate and efficient multi-task learning (MTL) framework that jointly performs segmentation and landmark detection for CMR. The proposed SLaDNet-GaB framework integrates a Segmentation and Landmark Detection Network (SLaDNet) with a Gradient-as-Bridge (GaB) loss. SLaDNet adopts a shared feature encoder and two separate decoders to generate segmentation and landmark predictions, respectively. Inter-Task Feature Fusion (ITFF) modules are inserted between the decoders at multiple resolution scales to facilitate bidirectional information exchange via channel-wise attention. Along with two intra-task losses, the dedicated GaB loss is further introduced during training to enforce inter-task anatomical consistency. Specifically, the loss guides the predicted landmarks toward the segmentation objective boundaries using gradient maps. We comprehensively evaluated the proposed method against both single- and MTL baselines on two public CMR datasets: a cine dataset (ACDC; 105/15/30 subjects for training/validation/testing) and a T1 mapping dataset (STONE; 150/20/40 subjects for training/validation/testing). SLaDNet-Gab outperformed the baselines in both segmentation (dice scores: 92.37/94.27% on ACDC/STONE, p < 0.05) and landmark detection (point-to-point distances: 2.22/1.51 voxels on ACDC/STONE, p < 0.05). For downstream tasks, the proposed method consistently achieved lower strain and T1 quantification errors than the other methods in most myocardial segments, with per-segment measurements closely agreeing with the manually derived values. Moreover, SLaDNet-GaB demonstrated relatively low training times (11.4/3.2 hours on ACDC/STONE) and an inference time of 6.12 msec./sample suitable for clinical adoption. The proposed multi-tasking method achieves improved accuracy in CMR segmentation, landmark detection, and downstream quantification, while maintaining high computational efficiency.

title: Dosimetric impact of intrafractional ocular motion in LINAC-based ocular SRS/SRT: Defining real-time eye-tracking thresholds.
abstract: Photon-based LINAC ocular stereotactic radiosurgery and stereotactic radiotherapy (SRS/SRT) offer a noninvasive treatment approach for ocular malignancies. However, intrafractional ocular motion can compromise target coverage because of steep dose gradients and small treatment margins. Although ocular position monitoring and motion-management techniques have been investigated previously, quantitative dosimetric guidance relating angular gaze deviation to target and OAR degradation in modern LINAC ocular SRS/SRT remains limited. To characterize the dosimetric effects of simulated gaze deviation in photon-based LINAC ocular SRS/SRT, identify planning and geometric factors associated with motion robustness, and derive dosimetrically informed gaze-deviation thresholds for real-time eye tracking. Ninety-eight previously generated photon-based ocular SRS/SRT plans were retrospectively analyzed for ocular motion robustness using an Eclipse scripting approach. Planning target volumes (PTVs) were derived from hybrid CT-MRI and synthetic datasets based on clinically treated plaque brachytherapy cases, with a median PTV of 2.37 cc in the primary cohort. An ocular motion model was developed to simulate gaze deviations from 0° to 30° across 36 sampled directions per deviation level while incorporating both rotational and translational globe motion. All plans were prescribed 25 Gy in one fraction. A total of 109, 368 simulated dose evaluations were analyzed in the primary D95-normalized cohort, with corresponding PTV D98-normalized plans used to evaluate the effect of prescription normalization. Additional paired subgroup analyses evaluated beam energy (6 MV FFF vs. 10 MV FFF), MLC configuration (standard MLC vs micro-MLC), and PTV margin size (2 vs. 1 mm). The primary robustness endpoint was maximum safe gaze deviation, defined using preservation of simulated V100 ≥ 90%. Additional analyses evaluated OAR doses and associations between baseline geometric and dosimetric variables and motion robustness. Target coverage progressively deteriorated with increasing simulated gaze deviation. Using V100 ≥ 90% as the prespecified target-coverage criterion, at least 75% of D95- and D98-normalized plans maintained acceptable worst-direction coverage through approximately 6° and 9°, respectively. Optic nerve D0.03 cm3 increased with gaze deviation, with the 75th percentile remaining at or below 12.1 Gy through approximately 7° for D95-normalized plans and 6° for D98-normalized plans. Lens D0.03 cm3 exceeded the 5-Gy reference threshold in most plans at baseline and was therefore not used to determine a motion threshold. Greater target distance from the globe center strongly predicted reduced motion robustness, whereas larger target volume was associated with greater robustness. Higher plan conformity was also associated with increased motion sensitivity. Beam energy, MLC configuration, PTV margin, and tumor directionality had less practical influence on the derived robustness thresholds. Photon-based LINAC ocular SRS/SRT demonstrated progressive target-coverage loss and increasing selected OAR doses with increasing simulated gaze deviation. Considering both target coverage and optic nerve dose, an approximately 5° gaze deviation represents a reasonable dosimetrically informed starting point for prospective real-time ocular motion monitoring. title: Impact of dose reduction and multi-parametric harmonization on multi-organ radiomics robustness in total-body PET imaging: Methodological implications for quantitative theranostics.
abstract: Radiomic features derived from positron emission tomography (PET) are sensitive to count statistics and acquisition protocol variability, thereby limiting quantitative reliability in low-dose and multi-center total-body PET imaging. This study evaluated dose robustness of PET radiomics and assessed the impact of multi-parameter ComBat harmonization on feature reproducibility. A multi-center total-body PET dataset comprising 550 patients from two institutions was retrospectively analyzed. Seven dose levels were simulated from list-mode data (Standard; dose reduction factors (DRF) of 2, 4, 10, 20, 50, and 100). Automatic deep learning-based segmentation was applied. A total of 107 Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomic features were extracted from standardized uptake value (SUV)-normalized images. Feature-level ComBat harmonization was performed under five configurations (scanner manufacturer, pixel spacing, radiopharmaceutical, scatter correction, and non-harmonized baseline). Reproducibility was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC (2,1)) across dose levels, organs, and harmonization settings. Dose reduction produced organ- and feature-dependent effects. Overall, 32.7% of the features achieved good or excellent reproducibility (ICC ≥ 0.75) in at least one anatomical region. Selected first-order and intensity-associated features retained good reproducibility in several anatomical regions under moderate dose reduction (DRF ≤ 20), whereas severe count reduction (DRF 50-100) was associated with greater organ- and feature-dependent instability, particularly among higher-order texture features in vascular and lower-contrast soft-tissue regions. Harmonization produced organ and feature-dependent changes but did not uniformly improve cross-dose reproducibility or compensate for noise-induced instability. Radiomics robustness in total-body PET is strongly influenced by dose level, anatomy, and acquisition variability. Moderate dose reduction preserves selected intensity-based features, while extreme count reduction compromises higher-order textures. Harmonization altered reproducibility patterns but did not uniformly improve cross-dose agreement or fully offset noise-induced instability, underscoring the need for dose-aware feature selection in multi-center PET radiomics.

title: A simple and interpretable method to predict head and neck offline adaptation needs based on anatomical changes.
abstract: Modern radiotherapy techniques do not automatically account for anatomical changes during treatment, which can lead to reduced target coverage, hotspots, or increased dose to healthy tissues. Adaptive Radiotherapy (ART) addresses this by updating the treatment plan based on the patient's current anatomy. In routine clinical practice, the decision to replan is often triggered by a suboptimal fit of the immobilization mask, identified by the radiation therapy technologist. Because this process is operator dependent and lacks methodological rigor, a quantitative decision-support method could substantially improve the replanning decision. Daily image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) images provide valuable clinical information but often lack sufficient quality for accurate target contouring or reliable dose calculation to support straightforward clinical decision-making. This limitation motivates the need for a simpler, more practical, and scalable alternative. This study develops an automated workflow to predict the need for replanning at every treatment fraction in head and neck (H&N) cancer patients using robust tools, thus requiring minimal manual validation while aiding the radio-oncologists in their decision-making. A retrospective dataset of 21 H&N cancer patients treated on a Tomotherapy Radixact system (Accuray, USA) with kVCT daily imaging was analyzed, of whom 14 underwent replanning during treatment. For each patient, the planning CT (pCT) and daily images were processed in RayStation treatment planning system (RaySearch Laboratories AB, Sweden) via scripts. Rigid registrations were used to align daily images to the pCT, and a patient-specific region of interest (ROI) was defined to consistently capture the same anatomical region across all treatment fractions. ROI volumes were intersected with the external contour and converted to relative volumetric changes with respect to the pCT. By grouping patients according to whether a replanning occurred during treatment, differences in mean volumetric change between replanned and non-replanned patients were assessed at each treatment fraction. To automatically detect clinically relevant anatomical changes, a simple, interpretable model based on three volumetric features (current volume loss, short-term trend, and long-term trend) was evaluated using cross-validation. Thresholds defining the trigger condition were optimized using a tailored loss function that prioritizes early detection and penalizes false negatives more strongly than false positives. Model variants using different feature subsets and hyperparameters were compared, and the final configuration was selected prioritizing recall, followed by specificity and early flagging. Significant differences in volumetric change between replanned and non-replanned patients emerged at fraction 6 and remained significant for most subsequent fractions. The smallest adjusted p -values occurred around fractions 22-25. Using leave-one-out cross-validation, the best-performing model flagged patients to be replanned with 93% recall, doing so on average 8.4 fractions before clinical intervention. Consistent differences in local tissue volume loss between replanned and non-replanned patients enabled the development of a simple automated workflow that triggers replanning for offline ART when learned volumetric thresholds are exceeded. This approach provides an objective complement to physician judgement and integrates seamlessly into existing IGRT workflows.

title: Segment anything model (SAM)-driven prompt-guided interactive delineation of gross tumor volume for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Segment Anything Model (SAM), a prompt-guided foundation model, exhibits substantial potential for medical image segmentation by incorporating prior knowledge through user-defined prompts. However, the application of SAM in radiotherapy target delineation remains limited. Purpose This study proposes a feasible prompt-guided interactive delineation workflow driven by an optimized SAM. Methods A total of 100 rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy cases were collected (60 for training and 40 for testing). This study utilized bounding-box prompts to guide SAM for GTV segmentation. Physicians manually draw box prompts on certain slices, while box prompts for the remaining slices are automatically generated using an interpolation strategy. Four fine-tuning strategies for SAM training were evaluated, and the impact of prompt numbers and placements was assessed as well. The performance of the finalized workflow with optimized SAM was compared with five state-of-the-art (SOTA) models, and its robustness to prompt variations in middle-slice selection and box-prompt margins was analyzed. Results Compared to other fine-tuning methods, freezing the image encoder obtained the most stable performance. Prompts on only 3 slices achieved accuracy comparable to prompts on all slices. The placement of the middle-slice prompt exhibited negligible impact (p > 0.05). The finalized SAM-driven workflow outperformed end-to-end baseline models both visually and quantitatively (3D DSC: 0.92 vs 0.80; 3D HD95: 2.73 vs 12.70; IoU: 0.86 vs 0.67; Sensitivity: 91.20% vs 85.98%; Precision: 93.65% vs 79.23%), while maintaining stable performance across certain prompt variations. Conclusions The proposed SAM-driven interactive workflow with as few as 3 box prompts achieves favorable accuracy of GTV segmentation for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.

title: Bilateral Breast Gradient Insert Prototype for Strong Diffusion Encoding at 3 T.
abstract: Purpose Diffusion MRI has shown promise for breast cancer screening, lesion characterization, and treatment response monitoring without contrast agents, but further translation is constrained by the gradient performance of conventional systems. The aim of this work is to develop a single-axis high-performance bilateral plug-and-play breast gradient insert to enable strong-gradient diffusion MRI. Methods An in-house breast gradient insert and bed-tabletop was constructed entirely from commercially available materials, providing a cost-effective solution compatible with existing MRI systems. Its wiring pattern was optimized for torque and force balancing, power dissipation, and target field performance. Evaluation included gradient field characterization, peripheral nerve stimulation simulation verification, and temperature and eddy current assessment. The setup was used for imaging of a diffusion phantom based on soy lecithin across a range of b values. Results Gradient efficiency ranged from 0.61 to 2.8 mT/m/A, enabling diffusion MRI using local strengths up to 420 mT/m (150 A). No peripheral nerve stimulation was observed during tests on five healthy volunteers. Eddy currents were successfully characterized, revealing a linear first order component with an amplitude of 0.03% of the applied gradient field. Imaging experiments demonstrated the feasibility of acquiring b = 10 000 s/mm 2 volumes with a TE of 78 ms, compared with 161 ms when using the scanner gradients (40 mT/m). Conclusion This work demonstrates a dedicated bilateral breast gradient insert for safe and feasible strong-gradient breast diffusion MRI and represents a first step toward dedicated hardware for breast cancer detection and characterization without contrast agents.

title: Independent Component Analysis for Non-Contrast-Enhanced Free-Breathing Pulmonary Ventilation and Perfusion MRI.
abstract: Purpose To introduce a robust approach for non-contrast-enhanced free-breathing functional lung MRI based on independent component analysis (ICA), addressing key limitations of standard methods such as sensitivity to irregular breathing or irregular heartbeat. Methods Repeated dynamic single-slice MRI of ten healthy volunteers and twenty-five lung tumor patients was performed in free breathing on a 0.35T MR-linac using a 2D coronal cine bSSFP sequence, resulting in 143 datasets. Following motion correction, lung segmentation, and signal alignment, temporal ICA was applied to extract ventilation and perfusion components. Ventilation- and perfusion-weighted maps were generated and compared to Fourier decomposition (FD) and matrix pencil (MP) analysis. Signal construction performance was evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient and nonparametric statistical testing, comparing the methods under regular and irregular breathing and heartbeat conditions. Map accuracy and robustness at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) were additionally assessed in numerical-phantom simulations. Results In vivo, ICA effectively separated physiological lung signals, achieving significantly higher temporal agreement with original voxel time courses than both FD and MP (all p<0.001 ). Under all physiological conditions, ICA yielded the highest temporal correlations. In simulations, ICA maintained robust signal fidelity, especially under irregular breathing and low-SNR conditions, preserving >90% of contrast in simulations, while FD and MP exhibited pronounced degradation and significantly reduced temporal correlations. Conclusion ICA functional lung MRI provides a robust alternative to conventional techniques, enabling reliable ventilation and perfusion assessment from free-breathing acquisitions, particularly in the presence of irregular respiratory patterns and motion.

title: Inertial Navigation Assisted Motion Correction for Brain MRI.
abstract: Purpose To assess the utility of inertial sensors for estimating parameters describing rigid body motion of the head, and to reduce motion related artifact through a hybrid prospective steering of the rotation via the sensor and retrospective realignment of translation via the MRI data. Theory and methods Inertial sensors are widely used for Earth navigation problems. However, drift accumulation from integrating noisy signals makes them impractical for MRI motion correction at millimeter resolution over minute-long scans. Prior work has shown that the MRI system's B0 and gravity are approximately orthogonal and can be exploited as reference vectors for 3-DOF orientation estimation. We introduce a hybrid inertial measurement-based method, which uses these fields to estimate 3-DOF orientation directly, without integration, thereby eliminating random walk. The remaining 3-DOF translation is recovered via phase correlation from the MRI data. We validate the efficacy of this hybrid method retrospectively using a 3D radial koosh-ball sequence and prospectively using 2D EPI time-series acquisition during volunteer motions. Results IMU-based orientation estimation followed by phase correlation achieved a mean accuracy of 0.6° and 0.4 pixels across all experiments. Image quality improved when motion correction was applied in all volunteer scans for both retrospective and prospective correction cases. Conclusion The proposed method measured head motion in the MRI scanner with high accuracy at unprecedented sampling rates and enabled both retrospective and prospective correction, improving image quality by aligning k-space data and reducing motion artifacts.

title: NR-MRC: A No-Reference Magnetic Resonance Curve Estimation Network for Tumor MR Image Quality Assessment and Enhancement.
abstract: Purpose Accurate image quality assessment (IQA) is essential for evaluating tumor magnetic resonance (MR) images in clinical practice and computer-aided diagnosis. However, most existing IQA models are designed for natural images and require reference images for training. Variability in tissue characteristics, lesion location, and lesion morphology, together with the scarcity of high-quality MR reference images, makes quality assessment of tumor MR images particularly challenging. Methods To address these challenges, we propose a no-reference magnetic resonance curve estimation network named NR-MRC. First, a magnetic resonance curve estimation module uses nonlinear curve mapping to estimate spatially adjusted intensity and detail features without requiring reference tumor MR images. Second, a multi-scale feature estimation module extracts contextual features at different scales and fuses them with the initial estimates to generate enhanced MR images. Finally, a magnetic resonance scene statistics blind quality model evaluates feature consistency between the original images and their enhanced counterparts. Results Experiments on publicly available brain tumor and bladder cancer datasets demonstrate that NR-MRC outperforms the compared IQA and image enhancement methods. In the tested U-Net and DeepLab v3 settings, training with images selected by high NR-MRC scores or enhanced by NR-MRC increased segmentation metrics by approximately 20%. These task-specific gains do not by themselves establish improved clinical diagnostic image quality. Conclusion NR-MRC provides no-reference quality assessment and enhancement for tumor MR images and shows potential utility in the evaluated downstream segmentation tasks.

title: Weakly Convex Ridge Regularization for 3D Non-Cartesian MRI Reconstruction.
abstract: While highly accelerated non-Cartesian acquisition protocols significantly reduce scan time, they often entail long reconstruction delays for 3D data. Deep learning-based reconstruction methods can alleviate this, but typically rely on complex, highly parametrized architectures. As an alternative, we introduce a rotation-invariant weakly convex ridge regularizer (WCRR). The resulting variational reconstruction approach is benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods on retrospectively simulated data and out-of-distribution prospective GoLF-SPARKLING and CAIPIRINHA acquisitions. Our approach achieves competitive reconstruction quality while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters and retaining the interpretability of a sparsity-promoting variational prior. In summary, WCRR provides a compact and interpretable learned variational prior for 3D non-Cartesian MRI reconstruction.

title: Clinical Correlations Between Diagnostic Assessment Methods and Functional Outcomes in Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Background Musculoskeletal disorders are major contributors to pain, disability, reduced participation, and health-care utilisation. Structural and digital diagnostic tools can characterise pathology, but their ability to explain functional limitations and rehabilitation prognosis is often incomplete. This narrative review aimed to synthesise representative evidence on the relationship between diagnostic and screening methods and functional outcomes in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, with emphasis on clinical interpretation and practical use in care pathways. Methods Peer-reviewed literature, supplemented by manual screening of relevant reference lists, was reviewed to identify publications available through March 2026. The synthesis prioritised studies linking diagnostic findings to patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), performance-based tests, or real-world activity metrics. Results Conventional imaging, including ultrasound, computed tomography, and MRI, may identify clinically relevant pathology but often shows only modest concordance with pain, disability, and performance-based function. PROMs and brief performance tests provide the most direct functional anchors, whereas interpretation using the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) or responder thresholds is needed to distinguish statistically detectable associations from clinically meaningful change. Biomarkers and AI-supported analytics remain promising but insufficiently validated for independent functional prognostication. Wearable sensors appear most clinically useful for longitudinal monitoring of real-world activity, and brief psychosocial screening helps explain the discordance between structural findings and perceived disability. Conclusion Functional prognosis in musculoskeletal rehabilitation should not rely on diagnostic findings alone. A multidimensional, function-centred first-visit bundle combining focused examination, one region-specific PROM, one brief performance test, and brief psychosocial risk screening may improve triage, patient communication, rehabilitation planning, and follow-up. Diagnostic escalation should be selective and reserved for red flags, management-changing pathology, or failure to improve on repeated standardised functional reassessment.
